content: Yersinia pestis is the bacterium responsible for causing bubonic plague, also known as the Black Death. During the incubation period of the disease, swollen lymph nodes, known as buboes, typically develop in the armpits and groin. These buboes form because the bacteria localize in the lymph nodes during infection. If left untreated, the infection can rapidly disseminate to other organs. Yersinia was previously classified under the Pasteurellaceae family but was reclassified into the Enterobacteriaceae family in 1995 based on DNA-DNA hybridization studies showing similarities to Escherichia coli. Differentiation of Enterobacteriaceae family members is based on biochemical and antigenic profiles, with nucleic acid techniques increasingly used to refine genus and species definitions. Among the 11 named species in the Yersinia genus, only three are significant human pathogens: Y. pestis, Y. pseudotuberculosis, and Y. enterocolitica. Y. pseudotuberculosis is the closest genetic relative to Y. pestis but can be distinguished by its clinical manifestations and laboratory test results. Y. pestis and Y. pseudotuberculosis rarely infect humans, whereas Y. enterocolitica is more commonly found in clinical specimens. A very small number of Y. pestis organisms are sufficient to infect mammals. As few as 1 to 10 organisms can cause infection in small mammals, such as rodents or primates, through subcutaneous, oral, intravenous, or intradermal routes. However, respiratory transmission requires a higher dose, approximately 100 to 200,000 organisms, for nonhuman primates. Upon entering the host, environmental signals such as elevated temperature, low pH within cells, and contact with eukaryotic cells are believed to trigger the synthesis of virulence factors in the bacteria. During the incubation phase, the hallmark symptom of bubonic plague, the bubo, arises as the bacteria spread to regional lymph nodes. If untreated, the infection progresses rapidly, leading to septicemia and dissemination to other organs. Septicemic plague often presents with cyanosis and necrosis, likely due to coagulase activity of the plasminogen activator. Commonly infected tissues include the liver, lungs, skin, mucous membranes, spleen, and, in late stages, the meninges. Yersinia pestis is a Gram-negative, facultative anaerobic, bipolar-staining bacillus (giving it a safety pin appearance) within the Enterobacteriaceae family. It produces an antiphagocytic slime layer and is motile when isolated but becomes nonmotile in mammalian hosts. Y. pestis infection can manifest as bubonic, pneumonic, or septicemic plague, all of which have historically caused high mortality rates during epidemics, including the Black Death, which killed approximately one-third of the European population between 1347 and 1353. The pathogenicity of Y. pestis is partly attributed to two antiphagocytic antigens, F1 (Fraction 1) and V, which are critical for virulence and produced at 37°C. The bacterium survives and produces these antigens within monocytes but not within polymorphonuclear neutrophils. Immunity, whether natural or induced, is achieved through the production of specific opsonic antibodies against F1 and V antigens, which promote phagocytosis by neutrophils. A formalin-inactivated vaccine was previously available for high-risk adults but was removed from the market due to limited effectiveness and potential for severe inflammation. Current research on genetically engineered vaccines targeting F1 and V antigens shows promise, though challenges remain due to the virulence of F1-lacking bacteria and variability in V antigens. The complete genomic sequences of two Y. pestis subspecies, strain KIM (biovar Medievalis) and strain CO92 (biovar Orientalis), are available. The chromosome of strain KIM is 4,600,755 base pairs long, while that of strain CO92 is 4,653,728 base pairs long. Y. pestis, like its relatives Y. pseudotuberculosis and Y. enterocolitica, carries the plasmid pCD1. Additionally, it hosts two other plasmids, pPCP1 and pMT1, which are absent in other Yersinia species. These plasmids, along with a pathogenicity island called HPI, encode proteins responsible for Y. pestis's virulence, including factors required for bacterial adhesion, injection of proteins into host cells, invasion, and iron acquisition from red blood cells. Y. pestis is thought to have evolved from Y. pseudotuberculosis, differing primarily in the presence of specific virulence plasmids. Traditional first-line treatments for Y. pestis include streptomycin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and fluoroquinolones. Doxycycline and gentamicin are also effective. However, strains resistant to one or two of these agents have been isolated, so treatment should be guided by antibiotic sensitivity testing when available.
